content: Body image refers to an individual's perception of their own physical appearance, as well as the internal sense of having a body, which is constructed by the brain. Essentially, body image is how a person perceives their external appearance, which can often differ significantly from how others perceive them. Negative feelings about one's body can sometimes lead to mental health disorders such as depression or eating disorders, although these conditions can arise from a variety of causes. In recent years, there has been significant debate within the media industry regarding the influence of Size Zero models on young people's body image. Critics argue that these models can contribute to feelings of insecurity about one's body. Some have even proposed banning Size Zero models from fashion runways. Public figures such as David Beckham, Victoria Beckham, Nicole Richie, and Beyoncé have been part of these discussions, as have other thin celebrities like British supermodel Kate Moss. While male celebrities have also been targeted in similar ways, the media's focus has predominantly been on the impact of the Size Zero phenomenon on young women. Body image is often assessed by asking individuals to rate their current and ideal body shapes using visual depictions. The difference between these ratings reflects the level of body dissatisfaction. Research by Monteath and McCabe found that 44% of women report negative feelings about both specific body parts and their overall bodies. A 1997 survey by Psychology Today revealed that 56% of women and approximately 40% of men were dissatisfied with their overall appearance. Poor body image is strongly correlated with the desire to lose weight, which is more common among women than men. However, studies by Susan Kashubeck-West, Laurie B. Mintz, and Ingrid Weigold suggest that gender differences in body image disappear when focusing solely on individuals actively trying to lose weight. Life orientation also influences body image. Women who identify as feminists tend to have a more positive view of their bodies compared to those who do not, despite no significant differences in average body weight between the groups. Factors such as exercise habits, sexual experiences, and mood also play a role in shaping body image. Men's body image has become an increasingly prominent topic in both academic research and popular media. Many men express a desire to become more muscular, often wishing for up to 26 pounds of additional muscle mass. This desire is closely linked to traditional concepts of masculinity. Research indicates a relationship between men's endorsement of traditional masculine ideals and their desire for increased muscle mass. This connection may begin early in life, as boys' action figures are often depicted with exaggerated, super-muscular physiques that exceed the limits of human physiology. The pursuit of additional muscle mass has been referred to by various terms, including The Adonis Complex, Bigorexia, Reverse Anorexia, and Muscle Dysmorphia. Dissatisfaction with muscle size has been associated with low self-esteem, personality disorders, and the use of muscle-building supplements and anabolic steroids. As such, body image dissatisfaction among men represents a significant concern for public health researchers. The concept of body image is deeply rooted in the brain's construction of a body-image, a term introduced by neurologist Henry Head and often used interchangeably with body-schema. The brain integrates input from the visual system, vestibular system, and proprioception (the sense of body position and movement) to create this body-image. Proprioception, a term coined by Charles Scott Sherrington, involves dynamic body maps in the somatosensory, motor, and parietal cortices. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1), where the sensory homunculus resides, plays a key role in processing cutaneous, visceral, and proprioceptive sensations. Sensory input travels from peripheral nerves, through the spinal cord, and into the brain to construct this body-image. Damage to sensory nerves that transmit proprioceptive input to the brain can result in a loss of proprioception, leading to a profound sense of disembodiment. For example, in Oliver Sacks' book The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat, he describes a patient named Christina who suffered from selective neuritis, an infection in her spinal fluid that disconnected her body from her brain's parietal cortices. This caused a total loss of proprioception, leaving her unable to control her limbs effectively. She experienced flailing movements, difficulty sitting or standing upright, and a sense of her body as disconnected and floppy. Phantom limb sensations are another phenomenon related to body-image. Many amputees continue to feel the presence of their missing limbs, as the brain's body-image remains intact. Even individuals born without certain limbs can experience phantom sensations. These sensations can be so vivid that patients may attempt to use their phantom limbs, such as stepping out of bed on phantom legs or picking up objects with a phantom hand. Phantom limbs are integral to the effective use of prosthetics, as the brain's body-image of the missing limb must align with the prosthetic for it to function properly. Phantom limbs can take various forms. Some are paralyzed or frozen in unusual positions, while others are exact replicas of the missing limb. In some cases, phantom limbs may be distorted, disproportionate, or even disconnected from the body, appearing to dangle in mid-air. Interestingly, some phantom limbs disappear only to reappear years later. There are even reports of women experiencing phantom penises with phantom erections, highlighting the complex interplay between body-image and brain function. The somatosensory system is also implicated in phantom limb syndrome. According to V.S. Ramachandran, motor signals contribute to the phenomenon. When the motor cortex sends signals to muscles, a duplicate signal is sent to the parietal lobes in a feedback loop, creating a sense of proprioception in the missing limb. Electrical stimulation of the angular gyrus can induce out-of-body experiences, decoupling vision and proprioceptive sensory input. Additionally, some patients with anosognosia, particularly those with left-side hemiplegia following a stroke, may deny ownership of their paralyzed limbs. They may perceive the limb as belonging to someone else or believe their real limb has disappeared, leading them to attempt to remove the foreign limb from their bed. This type of anosognosia is associated with lesions in the right somatosensory and parietal cortices.
